title: Knowledge Is Power, but the Charlatan Is More Credible
author: Jo Fujiwara
summary: Jo Fujiwara's essay argues that schools are addressing AI's effect on students at the wrong level, focused on usage-time policies and detection tools rather than the deeper question of what knowledge students need to resist being misled by fluent, confident-sounding AI output. Drawing on a 2025 study by Mark Steyvers on the 'calibration gap,' the piece shows that longer AI-generated explanations increase user confidence in an answer's accuracy without actually improving that accuracy, meaning polish and length function as false signals of credibility, exactly the charlatan's advantage referenced in the title. A second cited study, published in Science Advances, found that AI-assisted short stories became measurably more similar to one another (about 10.7 percent) than stories written without AI assistance, evidence for a homogenizing effect on collective creative output even as individual pieces improved. Fujiwara connects this to a broader concern that schools' AI policies regulate the tool but never articulate what students actually need to develop independent judgment, and argues the answer is not less AI exposure but more foundational knowledge, since a student who knows enough history, math, and literature can recognize when a fluent AI answer is thin or wrong. The essay closes by reframing 'knowledge is power' for the AI era: whoever controls the tools that shape perceived credibility gains disproportionate influence over what counts as true.
points: Cites Mark Steyvers's 2025 'calibration gap' research showing longer AI explanations increase user confidence without improving actual answer accuracy, a mechanism the essay argues favors fluent charlatans over substance.
Cites a Science Advances study finding AI-assisted short stories became about 10.7% more similar to each other than non-AI stories, evidence of a homogenizing effect on collective creative output.
Critiques current school AI policies for regulating usage minutes and detection rather than articulating what students need to develop independent, resistant judgment.
Argues the solution is more foundational subject knowledge, not less AI exposure, since knowledgeable students can recognize when fluent AI output is thin or unsupported.
quotes: The greater danger is not that AI takes credit for our thinking, but that the user gradually hands over the thinking itself.
We may be approaching not the optimum in informative writing, but rather a commercially and statistically preferred version of it.

In experiments using multiple-choice and short-answer questions, users tended to overestimate the accuracy of answers accompanied by the AI's explanations. The longer the explanations, the more people's confidence increased, even when the additional length did not improve the accuracy of the explanation.
Stories in the one-idea condition were about 10.7 percent more similar to one another than stories in the no-AI condition.
A system can pull many minds toward similar outputs and opinions, and convergence on the same answer is not, by itself, evidence that a population has become more intelligent.
We need to insist that knowledge is the material of thought, not an obsolete requirement of a test.
Let's teach enough literature that a student can hear whose voice is missing from a story.
